messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 41
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: Middle Eastern
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Fast Food Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 64

**Patient Vignette: "Tariq"**

Tariq is a 41-year-old single man who presents for therapy at the urging of his primary care doctor. He speaks with a quiet, measured tone, often pausing to look at the floor before answering questions. He has worked the closing shift at a fast-food restaurant for the past six years, a job he describes as “simple” and “safe.”

The event that changed everything happened fourteen months ago. Tariq was working the drive-thru window on a cool November night. At 10:47 PM, a customer in a sedan pulled up, paid, and then suddenly a man on a motorcycle stopped behind him. Tariq remembers the yelling first—two voices, sharp and fast in a language he didn’t fully understand. Then he heard a sound he had only ever heard in movies: a single gunshot, flat and final. The man on the motorcycle crumpled onto the pavement. Tariq watched the sedan speed away. He froze at the window, the credit card machine still buzzing in his hand. He did not scream. He did not run. He just stood there, watching the blood spread under the streetlight.

For three weeks after, Tariq did not sleep. He would lie in his small apartment, replaying the sound of the shot, the way the man’s helmet visor cracked. He began avoiding the drive-thru window, asking to work the fry station instead. His manager agreed, but Tariq could still hear the cars pulling up, the same engine sounds. He started flinching when a car backfired outside the restaurant. One night, a customer honked twice, and Tariq dropped a basket of fries, his heart pounding so hard he thought he might vomit.

Tariq’s social world has shrunk. He used to call his mother in Jordan every Sunday; now he lets the calls go to voicemail. He cannot bear to hear her voice because it reminds him of the fragility of life, of the man on the ground who never got to call his own mother again. He has stopped going to the mosque on Fridays because the crowded parking lot triggers memories of the sedan speeding away. He feels a constant, low-grade dread, as if something terrible is about to happen, even when he is home alone.

At work, Tariq is reliable but hollow. He performs his tasks mechanically—flipping patties, bagging orders, wiping counters—but he cannot remember the faces of his coworkers. He feels detached from his own body, as if he is watching himself from a distance. When a customer shouts at him for a missing item, he does not get angry; he just stares, his mind blank, his hands trembling. He has started drinking two or three beers after every shift to quiet the intrusive images, but the images only grow louder in the dark of his apartment.

Last month, Tariq saw a man in a red sedan at a stoplight and his chest tightened so severely that he had to pull over. He sat on the curb for twenty minutes, gasping, convinced he was having a heart attack. He went to the emergency room, but all tests came back normal. The doctor asked if he had been under stress. Tariq said no.

He does not speak of the shooting to anyone. He believes that if he talks about it, he will relive it fully, and he is not sure he would survive that. He has no close friends in the city, no partner. His life has become a narrow corridor of work, beer, and sleepless nights. He does not know why he is here, in this office. He only knows that his doctor said he had to come, and Tariq has always done what he was told.

He sits across from me now, his hands folded in his lap, his eyes fixed on a spot on the carpet. He is waiting for me to tell him what is wrong with him. I do not answer yet. I just sit with him in the quiet, letting him know that for the first time in fourteen months, someone is willing to witness his silence.
